newsitem.title: UK: UK budget seen too modest to halt consumer boom.
newsitem.headline: UK budget seen too modest to halt consumer boom.

text.p: UK Finance Minister Gordon Brown's first budget stands up to scrutiny in the cold light of day but financial markets and consumers are likely to face further interest rate rises, experts said on Thursday.

The economy is in good shape and public finances are improving rapidly. The problem is that within a budget that tightened fiscal policy by about 5.5 billion pounds ($9.2 billion), next to nothing was done to restrain the heady pace of high street spending.

Not true, protested Brown, in a post-budget briefing on Thursday. The reduction of tax relief on mortgage interest payments (MIRAS), a rise in stamp duty on expensive house purchases and increased excise duties on tobacco, petrol and alcohol represented a significant restraint, he said.
"If you look at that you will see I have done what is necessary to bring fiscal and monetary policy back into balance," Brown said.

But leading think-tank the Institute for Fiscal Studies said the effect of the cut in MIRAS and higher excise duties would cost the richest 10 percent of Britons only about two pounds a week, once the offsetting effect of a cut in sales tax on heating fuel to five percent was taken into account.
For poorer members of the population, the overall loss of income will be even smaller.
The measures are expected to have little impact on spending as millions of Britions enjoy a 30 billion pound bonanza from building society flotations.
"In the short-term, it has not done much to restrain demand," said Andrew Sentance, director of the London Business School's Centre for Economic Forecasting.
"The promise of a radical budget to rebalance the economy by squeezing consumer spending and encouraging investment has not been backed up," he said.
On the demand side, the ball is now firmly in the Bank of England's court. Its monetary policy committee, independent to set interest rates, meets next week.
Many economists see base rates climbing to eight percent, from 6.5 percent now.

That will do nothing to rectify the imbalance in the economy that Brown claims to have righted. Higher rates will mean a higher pound, which has already rocketed by about 20 percent since last August.
The further it climbs the more exporters' prices rise and the harder they find it to sell abroad. Manufacturers, and exporters in particular, already represent the weakest part of the economy.

The only saving grace for them has been the strength of domestic consumer demand, offsetting overseas weakness. Another round of rate rises -- there have already been two quarter-point jumps since Labour stormed to power on May 1 -- will cut domestic demand and push the pound higher still, a double blow for exporters.
Brown's other key pledge, aside from his centrepiece welfare-to-work programme, was to boost investment in a country traditionally deficient in that respect.
To that end he cut corporation tax by two percentage points to 31 percent. That would add about two billion pounds to corporate profits, Stephen Bond at the Institute for Fiscal Studies said.

But while giving with one hand Brown took more away with the other. The abolition of tax credits on Advance Corporation Tax, hitherto paid to pension funds and other institutions which are exempt from the tax, took five billion pounds out of the business sector, he said.

The tax break for pension funds encouraged them to hold equities and receive dividends free of tax. Brown believes that by closing that loophole, companies will be less inclined to pay huge dividends and more able to plough profits back.
"Despite Gordon Brown's rhetoric, it is difficult to see how the changes will help investment," Bond said.
Companies will still come under pressure to pay out large dividends. "Indeed they will be pressured to make up a substantial part of the five billion in lost revenues," he said.
The unequivocally good news for the markets in the budget was the healthy forecasts for public finances.
Brown forecast Britain's public sector borrowing requirement would fall to 13.3 billion pounds this financial year, then 5.4 billion next year and by early next century would be heavily in surplus.
"The lower PSBR forecasts for the next couple of years are good news," Briscoe said. "For now, on public finances at least, they can enjoy the benefits of an economy in good shape."
But what is good news for the markets may not be for the public sector as spending is cut.
Spending would have to fall to 38 percent of national income in 2001/2002 from 41 percent last year, the IFS said.

"To achieve this, we are talking about reductions in spending in real terms over the planning horizon -- about four billion pounds by the end of the century," John Hall at the think-tank said. ($ = 0.596 British Pounds)
